analysis.one_liner: Bans employers from forcing workers into mandatory arbitration to settle job disputes.
analysis.headline: A bill to ban forced arbitration of workplace disputes drew 59 House Democrats and died without a single committee vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Most large employers require new hires to sign agreements saying that if the company cheats them on pay or discriminates against them, the worker cannot go to court or join a class action — the dispute must be settled privately, one worker at a time, in front of an arbitrator chosen under employer-friendly rules. In May 2018 the Supreme Court upheld those clauses (Epic Systems v. Lewis), holding that federal arbitration law overrides laws that let workers sue together. H.R. 7109, the Restoring Justice for Workers Act, would have reversed that: employers could no longer force workers to agree to arbitration as a condition of being hired. Arbitration would still be allowed, but only if the worker agreed after a dispute actually happened, in writing, in plain language, without coercion, and an employer could not punish a worker for refusing. The bill was referred to the Judiciary and Education and Labor committees, then to a Judiciary subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 60 million U.S. workers covered by forced arbitration clauses, and any worker with a wage, discrimination, or safety claim. Workers would regain the right to take their case to court and, crucially, to join class or collective actions — the bill's text notes that class action is often the only economically realistic way an employee can challenge a wage violation, and that many workers with claims seek no redress at all once arbitration is forced on them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers who signed away their day in court

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits employers from requiring workers to sign pre-dispute arbitration agreements covering employment disputes, so the arbitration clause cannot be a condition of getting or keeping a job.

Restores workers' ability to bring or join class and collective actions, which the bill's findings describe as often the only way an employee can realistically pursue a claim; under the Supreme Court's Epic Systems decision, mandatory clauses already force workers to waive that right.
Still permits arbitration, but only as a voluntary, post-dispute choice: the worker must enter it without coercion and be informed in writing, in plain language, of the rights the agreement gives up.
Makes it illegal for an employer to retaliate against an employee for refusing to agree to arbitration.

analysis.who_pays: Employers that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses — they would face court litigation, class actions, and higher, more public liability for wage and discrimination violations, instead of private one-on-one arbitration. Private arbitration firms would also lose the steady stream of employment cases that pre-dispute clauses funnel to them.

drawbacks.text: Employers and arbitration's defenders argue that workers consent to these clauses in a signed employment contract and that arbitration is faster and cheaper for an individual worker than a years-long court case.

An honest supporter would concede that banning pre-dispute clauses raises litigation costs for employers of every size, costs that can be passed on in prices or hiring, and that some low-value individual claims may settle less often in court. The bill does not address those costs directly.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and broad: workers regain access to the courts and to class actions for wage theft and discrimination, and the bill's own findings state that many workers with valid claims currently pursue no redress at all once arbitration is forced on them. The cost falls on employers in the form of litigation exposure and on arbitration providers, and is partly offset by the bill's design, which preserves arbitration as a voluntary option after a dispute arises rather than banning it outright.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee — never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote in either the Judiciary or Education and Workforce committee — and died when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Jerrold Nadler (D-NY) introduced the bill on October 30, 2018, about five months after the Supreme Court's Epic Systems v. Lewis decision, which the bill's findings respond to.
58 House Democrats cosponsored it; no Republicans did.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and to the Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day it was introduced.
On November 15, 2018 it was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law — the last action ever taken on it.
No hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses kept the status quo the Supreme Court had just upheld in Epic Systems: they can still require workers to waive court access and class actions as a condition of employment, and private arbitration providers kept their case flow. Workers who signed forced arbitration clauses stayed right where they were.

for.name: Rep. Jerrold Nadler (D-NY)
for.role: Sponsor; senior member and former ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee

for.name: 58 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of the 58 cosponsors was a Republican

against.name: House Republican leadership and committee chairs
against.role: Controlled which bills got hearings and floor time in the 115th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or a floor vote; it received no action beyond referral and subcommittee referral

against.name: Business groups favoring arbitration clauses
against.what_they_did: Opposed efforts to roll back forced arbitration for employment disputes, favoring the Epic Systems status quo

sides.party_line_note: All 59 supporters (the sponsor plus 58 cosponsors) were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-controlled House gave the bill no committee action or vote.

industries.industry: Large employers (all industries using mandatory arbitration clauses)
industries.note: The bill would have stripped them of the tool that lets them settle wage, discrimination, and safety claims privately and one worker at a time, out of court and away from class actions. Their interest in keeping the status quo runs directly against workers' ability to sue.

Pre-dispute mandatory clauses are the mechanism that routes employment disputes to paid arbitrators instead of courts; the bill keeps post-dispute voluntary arbitration but eliminates the guaranteed stream of cases that comes from clauses workers must sign to get hired.
